title: Destructuring, Spread and Template Literals
objective: After this lesson you will be able to unpack objects and arrays with destructuring patterns (rename, defaults, nested, skip, rest), copy and merge with spread knowing its one-level depth and later-keys-wins order, and build strings with template literals instead of concatenation chains.
why: This trio is the everyday grammar of modern codebases: React components pull props apart with destructuring, every state update is a spread merge, every log line and URL is a template literal — and API design in JavaScript converged on one destructured options object precisely because positional arguments stop reading at three parameters. The mechanics are small; the payoff is that data transforms become one declarative line instead of a mutate-and-hope paragraph. And the traps are real: defaults that skip null, copies that share their insides (Lesson 3's rule), merges whose winner flips with order — all covered here.

blocks.text: Destructuring: unpack where the data arrives

Most data arrives wrapped: a response object, a config object, a row from a table. Destructuring is the language's *unpack* operator — a pattern on the left of an `=` (or in a parameter list) that declares exactly which pieces you intend to use, by name. It replaces the three-line `const title = course.title; const hours = course.hours;` ritual with one line, self-documents what a function actually consumes, and — because it is a pattern — carries superpowers: renaming, defaults, and digging into nested shapes.

blocks.code:
const course = { title: 'SQL Basics', hours: 12, level: 'beginner' };

const { title, hours } = course;                 // basic: pull properties out by name
const { level: difficulty } = course;            // rename: level's VALUE lands in `difficulty`
const { track: trackName = 'general' } = course; // rename + default: track is missing → 'general'

console.log(title, '|', hours); // "SQL Basics | 12"
console.log(difficulty);        // "beginner"
console.log(trackName);         // "general" — defaults catch missing keys
blocks.caption: Destructuring declares the shape you expect — missing keys become undefined, defaults catch them
Nested patterns dig straight to the leaves — intermediate names are paths, not bindings

blocks.text: Three rules cover the fine print. **Defaults fire only for `undefined`** — a missing key, a hole in an array, an omitted argument. `null` is a deliberate, present value and sails straight through (`{ level = 'x' }` against `{ level: null }` gives you `null`) — the same rule, and the same API-consumer trap, as function defaults in Lesson 2. **Destructuring a null or undefined source throws** a `TypeError` — which is why parameter patterns pair with a `= {}` default, two blocks down. And in nested patterns, **intermediate names are paths** — `meta: { minutes }` reads `lesson.meta.minutes` without ever creating a `meta` binding.
Array destructuring: position is the pattern

blocks.caption: Holes skip, defaults fill, and the classic no-temp swap works because the right side is fully evaluated first

blocks.text: Arrays have no keys, so the pattern is positional: the *n*th binding receives the *n*th element, and a bare comma-pair (a *hole*) skips an index without binding it. The swap is the famous application: the right-hand side `[b, a]` is a brand-new array, fully built from the current values **before** any assignment happens, and then its elements are assigned left to right — which is why no temp variable is needed. One style note you will thank me for later: keep your semicolons — a line starting with `[` after a line without one gets parsed as a member access on the previous expression, and the resulting error will not point anywhere helpful.

blocks.caption: The = {} default exists for exactly one caller: renderCard() with no argument at all

blocks.text: This is the pattern that ended the positional-arguments era. A call like `renderCard({ title: 'SQL Basics', hours: 0 })` reads at the call site, survives new options being added (no more `fn(x, undefined, undefined, true)`), and is order-free. It also retires the 2013 idiom this lesson is here to bury: `options = options || {}; const hours = options.hours || 6;` — two bugs in two lines, because `||` fires on *every falsy value*, so `hours: 0` or `label: ''` is silently replaced by the default. Destructuring defaults fire only on `undefined` — real data survives. (The `||`-vs-`??` story gets the full treatment in Lesson 6.)
Rest vs spread: the same three dots, opposite directions

blocks.caption: Same three dots, opposite jobs: gather on the pattern side, scatter on the value side
Which direction do the dots point?
nodes: You see ... in a destructuring pattern or a parameter list — the LEFT side of an =, or inside ( ) parameters
→ REST: gathers the leftover values into ONE new array or object
You see ... inside an array/object literal, a function call's arguments, or a tagged template
→ SPREAD: scatters ONE iterable's values out into the surrounding slots
One mnemonic: rest collects what is left; spread hands out what you have

blocks.text: Spread for arrays: copy, merge, and borrow from iterables

blocks.caption: Spread merges arrays, copies them one level deep (Lesson 3's rule), and splits strings into characters

blocks.text: Spread for objects: merge with later-keys-wins order

blocks.caption: A merge is copy + override, and the override direction is decided purely by order

blocks.text: Each spread writes its properties in order, overwriting any same-named key it has already seen — so `{ ...defaults, ...overrides }` is the canonical defaults-then-user merge, and flipping the operands flips the winner for every shared key. You can exploit that on purpose: spread a literal LAST to force a value (`{ ...user, role: 'admin' }`) or FIRST to make it overridable. Two carry-overs from Lesson 3 apply to every spread, arrays included: the copy is **one level deep** (elements that are objects are shared with the original), and none of this is a deep copy — `structuredClone` remains the tool for full independence.
Template literals: strings with expressions inside

blocks.caption: Backticks, ${} expressions, real newlines — the end of 'a + b + "..."' chains

blocks.code:
let count = 0;
const label = `count: ${++count}`; // the expression runs NOW — when the literal is built
count = 99;                         // later changes do not rewrite finished templates
console.log(label, '| count is now', count); // "count: 1 | count is now 99"
blocks.caption: Template literals are evaluated eagerly, once, where they are written

blocks.text: Everything inside `${}` is an expression, evaluated **eagerly** at the moment the literal is built — arithmetic, method calls, even ternaries. That eagerness is the one behavior to internalize: a stored template is frozen text, and rebuilding it is how you refresh it (a label built before a mutation still shows the pre-mutation value, as the demo proves). Keep the expressions small and pure — a template that calls a function with side effects hides a call inside what looks like a string. Beyond interpolation, backtick strings hold **real newlines** (no `\n` stitching), and a function can be *tagged* onto a template to receive the raw pieces — the machinery behind styled-components and safe SQL helpers; library territory, but now you know what you are looking at.

blocks.title: Lesson 4 in six lines
items: Object destructuring pulls by name with superpowers: `const { level: difficulty, track = 'general' } = course` renames with `:` and defaults on undefined — null passes through untouched
Nested patterns dig to the leaves; intermediate names are paths, not bindings — and destructuring a null/undefined source throws, which is why parameter patterns carry `= {}`
Array destructuring binds by position: holes skip elements (`[first, , third]`), defaults fill missing slots, and `[a, b] = [b, a]` swaps because the right side is fully built first
Destructured parameters are the named-arguments pattern — `({ title = 'x' } = {})` — and they retire `options = options || {}` plus its falsy-erasing `||` chains
Rest gathers leftovers into one new array/object (pattern side); spread scatters one iterable into many slots (value side) — same three dots, opposite directions

Object spread merges with later-keys-wins (`{ ...defaults, ...user }`), copies exactly one level (Lesson 3), and template literals interpolate expressions eagerly at build time with real multi-line output

blocks.q: How do you design a function that takes a lot of optional configuration — and what are the honest trade-offs of the options-object pattern?
blocks.a: The pattern is one object parameter, destructured in the signature with defaults: `function search({ query, page = 1, pageSize = 20, sort = 'relevance' } = {})`. What it buys: call sites become self-documenting and order-independent — `search({ pageSize: 50, query: 'ts' })` reads, and new options can be added without touching existing callers, which positional arguments can never offer past three parameters. The costs, honestly: the signature stops advertising required values at the call site (TypeScript fixes exactly this), a forgotten `= {}` makes the zero-argument call throw a TypeError while destructuring undefined, and defaults fire only for undefined — a caller passing null deliberately skips them. The pre-ES2015 idiom it replaces — `options = options || {}; const page = options.page || 1` — has the same shape but an extra bug: `||` fires on every falsy value, so `page: 0` or `label: ''` silently becomes the default, where destructuring defaults treat them as real data. My rule of thumb: more than two parameters, or any optionality, and the object wins; positional stays for tight pairs like (x, y) or (key, value).

exercise.prompt: Modernize a 2013 helper without changing what it means. `makeLabel` below defaults its options with `||` chains and builds its string with `+` — and it carries one silent bug: `makeLabel({ hours: 0 })` erases the 0. Rewrite it with parameter destructuring and defaults plus a template literal, so the same three calls print `Untitled (6h, beginner)`, `SQL Basics (6h, beginner)` and — the fix — `Untitled (0h, beginner)`. Then add the two tools a modern options function deserves: `mergeConfig(base, overrides)` returning a merged object where overrides win (mutating neither input), and `report(config)` returning a two-line template literal.
hints: Move the defaults into the signature: `function makeLabel({ title = COURSE_DEFAULTS.title, hours = COURSE_DEFAULTS.hours, level = COURSE_DEFAULTS.level } = {})` — destructuring defaults fire only on undefined, which is exactly why `hours: 0` will survive.
The body becomes one template literal: `` `${title} (${hours}h, ${level})` `` — no `+` chains, no spacing surprises.

`mergeConfig` is one expression — `{ ...base, ...overrides }` — later spreads win and neither input is touched. `report` destructures `{ title, hours, level }` and uses a real newline inside the backticks.
exercise.why: The rewrite is a behavior fix disguised as a syntax upgrade. Destructuring defaults fire only when a key is undefined, so `hours: 0` — a real, present value — finally survives where `options.hours || 6` erased it, and the `= {}` default absorbs the zero-argument call that would otherwise throw while destructuring undefined. `mergeConfig` exploits later-keys-wins: each spread overwrites matching keys from earlier ones, so overrides legitimately win while both inputs stay untouched (the printed `base.retries` proves it). And `report` shows the two template-literal superpowers at once — `${}` interpolation with destructured names, and real newlines, which is why one literal prints two lines.

quiz.q: const { n: name } = { n: 'Ada' }; — after this line, what exists?
options: Both name and n, each holding 'Ada'
Only name — 'Ada'; n was just a path into the source object, and no n binding is created
Only n — 'Ada'; name is the path
A SyntaxError — you cannot rename while destructuring
quiz.explain: In `{ n: name }`, the left side of each colon is the KEY to read and the right side is the NEW binding: the value of n lands in name, and n itself is never a variable — checking `typeof n` gives "undefined" (the undeclared probe from Lesson 1). Renaming exists precisely because the source key may be a poor variable name (level → difficulty) or collide with an existing binding. Option 3 reverses the direction, and option 4 invents a restriction — renaming is core syntax.

quiz.q: const [first, , third] = [98, 75, 62, 40]; — what are first and third?
options: first is 98, third is 75 — bindings fill sequentially regardless of holes
first is 98, third is 62 — the bare comma (a hole) skips index 1 without binding it
first is 98, third is undefined — the pattern stops at the hole
SyntaxError — array patterns cannot contain empty slots
quiz.explain: Array patterns bind by position, and a hole advances the position counter without creating a binding: first takes index 0 (98), the hole skips index 1 (75), third takes index 2 (62). Option 1 forgets that holes advance the cursor; option 3 invents a short-circuit — the pattern happily continues past holes; and holes in patterns are standard syntax, so option 4 is wrong. Holes are how you grab the pieces you want from positional data like CSV rows or destructured `split()` output.

quiz.q: const { title, ...rest } = { title: 'Deep Dive', hours: 8, level: 'advanced' }; — what is rest?
options: An array of the remaining values: [8, 'advanced']
A new object holding every other own enumerable property: { hours: 8, level: 'advanced' }
The same object minus its title — rest IS the original, mutated
undefined — rest only works in array patterns
quiz.explain: Object rest collects every own enumerable property not matched by an earlier pattern name into a FRESH object — keys and values included: { hours: 8, level: 'advanced' }. It is a copy, not a mutation (option 3), it is an object because the source is an object (option 1 is the ARRAY form's behavior), and it works in both pattern kinds (option 4). Together with spread it powers the omit-one-key idiom: `const { internal, ...public } = config;`.

quiz.q: const merged = { ...defaults, ...user }; — both objects have a theme key. Whose theme is in merged, and why?
options: defaults' — the first spread claims the keys
user's — each spread writes in order, and a later spread overwrites same-named keys from earlier ones
Both, as an array: [defaultsTheme, userTheme]
It depends on which value is truthy
quiz.explain: Object spread applies properties sequentially: defaults' keys are written first, then user's keys overwrite every matching name — so user's theme wins purely by position. Flip the order ({ ...user, ...defaults }) and defaults wins; that is the whole later-keys-wins rule, and it is why the canonical merge puts defaults FIRST and user input LAST. Option 4 invents truthiness logic — order decides, never the values; and option 3 is not a thing JavaScript does.

quiz.q: Why does the parameter pattern in function render({ title } = {}) carry the = {} default?
options: It converts undefined property values to null
Without it, the call render() would throw a TypeError while trying to destructure undefined — the = {} hands the pattern an empty object to read from
It makes the function immune to extra properties in the options object
It is required syntax — destructured parameters cannot appear without a default
quiz.explain: Destructuring a null or undefined SOURCE throws a TypeError — the pattern needs an object to read from. render() passes no argument, so the parameter is undefined; the = {} default substitutes an empty object, from which title simply reads as undefined (and its own = default, if any, fires). Option 2 is the exact mechanism, option 4 is false (the default is optional — it just changes which calls work), and option 3 confuses this with rest patterns collecting leftovers.

summary: Destructuring unpacks by pattern: objects by key — with `rename:` aliases, `= default`s that fire only on undefined, and nested paths whose intermediate names are not bindings; arrays by position — with holes to skip, defaults for missing slots, and the swap `[a, b] = [b, a]` that works because the right side is fully built first. Function signatures destructure their options object — `({ title = 'x' } = {})` — the named-arguments pattern that retired `options = options || {}` and its falsy-erasing `||` chains. The same three dots point in opposite directions: rest gathers leftovers into a new array/object on the pattern side; spread scatters an iterable's values into literals and calls on the value side — merging with later-keys-wins, copying exactly one level (Lesson 3's rule, arrays included). Template literals interpolate expressions eagerly at build time and hold real newlines; concatenation chains are retired.
next: Your value toolkit is nearly complete — but data arrives in lists, and list processing has its own grammar. Next lesson: the array methods that replaced the manual for-loop — map to transform, filter to select, reduce to collapse — plus the method that mutates its caller (sort), the one that compares strings when you meant numbers, and the pipeline habits that keep a five-stage data transform readable and debuggable.
